questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Institutions of an early medieval kingdom
questions.learningObjective: Identify the role of a medieval assembly
questions.stem: A design brief for a museum exhibit asks which body advised an early medieval king on war and law

options.text: A council of nobles and bishops that met at the royal court
options.misconception: confuses a modern parliament with a medieval court council

options.text: A standing army that also handled legal appeals
options.misconception: treats military force as a deliberative institution

options.text: An assembly of landholders summoned only in emergencies
A single minister appointed for life by the pope
options.misconception: overstates papal control of royal administration

questions.explanation: The early medieval king relied on a broad assembly of landholders for major decisions, not a permanent body. Option A describes a later court council, while B and D misstate the institutional form.
questions.hint: Think of a summoned gathering rather than a fixed office.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a medieval charter is for
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a medieval charter
questions.stem: A design brief asks why a medieval lord would pay to have a charter written and sealed

answer.exemplar: A charter created a written, sealed record of a grant or privilege that could be shown to later rulers and courts, turning an oral promise into durable legal proof for the beneficiary.

questions.explanation: The charter's value lay in durable proof of a grant. Oral promises faded, but a sealed document could be presented to successors and courts.
questions.hint: Focus on proof and durability, not on the writing itself.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The conflict between crown and papacy over appointments

stimulus.body: A twelfth-century source notes that bishops received both ring and staff from the emperor while the pope claimed the right to choose them. The dispute reshaped church and state relations for decades.

questions.stem: A design brief cites a source where the emperor gives bishops ring and staff while the pope claims choice rights

options.text: It describes a quarrel over who may appoint bishops and abbots
It records a dispute about taxing church lands in Rome
options.misconception: confuses appointment rights with fiscal claims

options.text: It shows a debate about translating scripture into German
options.misconception: imports a later Reformation issue into the twelfth century

options.text: It proves bishops were elected by popular vote
options.misconception: reads modern elections into medieval selection

questions.explanation: The ring and staff symbolised spiritual office, so the clash concerned investiture. Taxation, translation, and popular election are not what the symbols denote.
questions.hint: Ring and staff stand for spiritual office, not money or language.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The function of an imperial chancery
questions.stem: A design brief asks what an imperial chancery mainly produced and why it mattered

options.text: It collected taxes directly from every village
options.misconception: confuses record keeping with revenue collection

options.text: It drafted and authenticated royal documents and charters
It trained knights for border defence
options.misconception: mistakes a writing office for a military academy

options.text: It judged criminal cases in the capital

questions.explanation: The chancery's core task was preparing and sealing royal documents. Tax collection, military training, and courts belonged to other offices.
questions.hint: Think of the office that writes and seals, not the one that fights or judges.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The legal position of a free city
questions.stem: A design brief needs the status of a city that answered only to the emperor

options.text: It owed military service only to its local bishop
It was subject to a territorial prince like other towns
options.misconception: treats a free city as an ordinary subject town

options.text: It had no obligations of any kind to anyone
It answered directly to the emperor, not to a prince

questions.explanation: A free imperial city owed allegiance to the emperor alone. It still had duties, and it was not under a prince or bishop.
questions.hint: Direct subjection to the emperor, not absence of duty.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The confessional rule of 1555
questions.stem: A design brief asks what the 1555 settlement let a territorial prince decide

answer.exemplar: The Peace of Augsburg let each territorial prince choose either Lutheranism or Catholicism for his lands, so subjects followed their ruler's confession rather than a single empire-wide faith.

questions.explanation: The settlement tied a territory's religion to its prince's choice. It did not grant individual freedom of conscience across the empire.
questions.hint: The prince's choice set the territory's religion.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The cause of the peasant revolts of 1524 and 1525

stimulus.body: A chronicler records that villagers refused new labour dues, cited old customs, and demanded relief from rising rents while lords enforced stricter collection.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes a chronicler on refused labour dues, old customs and rising rents

options.text: A single foreign invasion sparked all the uprisings
options.misconception: reduces a complex revolt to one external trigger

options.text: Economic pressure and disputes over customary rights drove the unrest
The peasants wanted to abolish all private property
The revolts began because printing presses stopped working
options.misconception: confuses economic grievance with a technology failure

questions.explanation: The chronicler points to labour dues, rents, and customary rights. Foreign invasion, property abolition, and press failure are not supported.
questions.hint: Look for grievances about dues, rents, and custom.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The cost of a territorial state
questions.stem: A design brief asks why building a territorial state proved expensive

options.text: It cost nothing because subjects served for free
options.misconception: assumes pre-modern states ran without expense

options.text: It needed only a single tax collector in the capital
options.misconception: underestimates the reach of territorial rule

options.text: It depended solely on volunteer nobles
options.misconception: ignores paid officials and standing forces

options.text: It required armies, courts, and administration across the land

questions.explanation: Territorial states needed military, judicial, and bureaucratic structures everywhere. A single collector, volunteers, or free service would not suffice.
questions.hint: State building means institutions spread across territory.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The purpose of the general estate tax
questions.learningObjective: State the purpose of a general estate tax
questions.stem: A design brief asks why rulers introduced a general tax on estates

options.text: To abolish all private land ownership
To fund standing armies and central administration
To reward only the clergy with exemptions
options.misconception: reduces a general tax to a clerical privilege

options.text: To replace every local custom with one law

questions.explanation: General estate taxes financed central needs such as armies and administration. They did not abolish property, favour only clergy, or unify law.
questions.hint: Revenue for central state needs, not property reform.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The printed press and the Enlightenment
questions.stem: A design brief asks how the printed press aided the Enlightenment

answer.exemplar: Cheaper printed books and pamphlets let ideas travel beyond courts and universities, so Enlightenment arguments reached a wider literate public and could be debated openly.

questions.explanation: Printing lowered the cost and raised the reach of ideas. The effect was wider debate, not just faster copying of older texts.
questions.hint: Think reach and cost, not just speed of copying.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The equality established in 1804

stimulus.body: A code from 1804 declared that all citizens were equal before the law and abolished feudal privileges, while property rights remained strongly protected.

questions.stem: A design brief cites an 1804 code that declares legal equality and abolishes feudal privileges

options.text: It ended all private property distinctions
It granted universal suffrage to all adults
options.misconception: confuses legal equality with voting rights

options.text: It established equality before the law for citizens
It made every citizen a noble by birth

questions.explanation: The 1804 code proclaimed legal equality and ended feudal privilege, but kept property. Suffrage, property abolition, and nobility are not what it established.
questions.hint: Legal equality before the law, not voting or property abolition.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a grant formula does
questions.stem: A design brief asks what a grant formula in a charter actually does

options.text: It records the weather on the signing day
options.misconception: treats a legal clause as a diary entry

options.text: It lists the price paid in silver coins
options.misconception: confuses the operative clause with a price list

options.text: It names the scribe who copied the text
options.misconception: mistakes a formula for an attribution

options.text: It states the legal act by which a right is transferred

questions.explanation: A grant formula expresses the legal transfer itself. Price, scribe, and weather are incidental details, not the operative clause.
questions.hint: The clause that performs the transfer, not surrounding details.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A grant of market rights
questions.stem: A design brief asks what a grant of market rights allowed a town

options.text: It could mint its own gold currency freely
options.misconception: confuses market rights with minting rights

options.text: It could hold a regular market with tolls and rules
It could ignore all royal taxes forever
options.misconception: overstates a market grant into tax immunity

options.text: It could draft citizens into a standing army
options.misconception: confuses commercial privilege with military duty

questions.explanation: Market rights let a town hold markets under set rules and tolls. Minting, tax immunity, and conscription are separate privileges.
questions.hint: Commerce and tolls, not money, taxes, or soldiers.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A figure in a chronicle
questions.stem: A design brief asks why a chronicle figure matters as a source

answer.exemplar: A chronicle figure such as a regnal year or event date anchors the narrative in time, letting readers sequence events and check the account against other dated sources.

questions.explanation: Dates and regnal years provide chronological anchors. Without them a chronicle is harder to verify or sequence.
questions.hint: Anchors the story in time for checking and sequencing.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The order of two past events

stimulus.body: A source states that a charter was issued in 1215 and a battle followed in 1216. The charter's terms mention the king's upcoming campaign.

questions.stem: A design brief cites a charter issued in 1215 and a battle in 1216

options.text: Both events happened in the same year
The battle caused the charter to be written
The charter precedes the battle by one year
The charter was written after the battle ended
options.misconception: places a later event before an earlier one

questions.explanation: 1215 comes before 1216, so the charter precedes the battle. Reversing or merging the dates contradicts the source.
questions.hint: Compare 1215 and 1216 directly.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a charter is read against
questions.stem: A design brief asks what a charter must be read against to be understood

options.text: The current exchange rate of its currency
The modern constitution of the same country
The personal diary of the scribe alone
The legal and political context of its issuing time

questions.explanation: A charter makes sense in its own legal and political setting. Modern constitutions, diaries, and exchange rates distort its meaning.
questions.hint: The setting of the time, not today's frameworks.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Why the Peace of Augsburg is called a settlement
questions.learningObjective: Explain the Peace of Augsburg as settlement
questions.stem: A design brief asks why the 1555 Peace of Augsburg counts as a settlement

options.text: It created a single religion for the whole empire
It paused religious war by letting princes choose a confession
It expelled all non-Catholics from imperial cities
It abolished the office of emperor entirely
options.misconception: confuses religious settlement with regime change

questions.explanation: The settlement ended fighting by allowing princely choice of confession. It did not impose one religion, expel groups, or abolish the emperor.
questions.hint: A pause through princely choice, not uniformity.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What an archive takes in
questions.stem: A design brief asks what an archive primarily takes in and keeps

answer.exemplar: An archive receives records of enduring value, appraises and describes them, and preserves them so that future researchers can verify claims and trace institutional decisions.

questions.explanation: Archives select and preserve records for future use. Their role is custody and description, not creating new records.
questions.hint: Custody and preservation of selected records.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The steps in the making of a charter

stimulus.body: A workshop manual describes drafting a charter, having it sealed by the issuer, and then delivering it to the recipient, with witnesses present at sealing.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes a manual on drafting, sealing and delivering a charter

options.text: Delivery happens before sealing in every case
Only sealing matters; drafting is optional
options.misconception: ignores the need for a drafted text

options.text: Drafting, sealing, and delivering are the main steps
Witnesses are forbidden from attending sealing

questions.explanation: The manual lists drafting, sealing, and delivery as steps. Drafting is needed, sealing precedes delivery, and witnesses attend.
questions.hint: Draft, seal, deliver, with witnesses at sealing.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Turning an interest into an archival question
questions.stem: A design brief asks how to turn a vague interest into an archival question

options.text: Replace the question with a list of famous names
options.misconception: substitutes names for an evidence question

options.text: Keep it as broad as possible to find everything
options.misconception: a broad question yields unfocused searching

options.text: Ask only for the oldest document in the archive
Narrow it to specific records, period, and evidence sought

questions.explanation: A workable question specifies records, period, and evidence. Breadth, age alone, or name lists do not focus the search.
questions.hint: Specific records, period, and evidence.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The fate of the 1848 constitution
questions.stem: A design brief asks what happened to the 1848 constitution

options.text: It became the permanent law of a unified Germany
options.misconception: confuses a draft with enacted constitution

options.text: It was rejected and never took effect
It was adopted unchanged by the Weimar Republic
options.misconception: imports a later constitution back to 1848

options.text: It abolished the monarchy by popular decree

questions.explanation: The 1848 constitution was not implemented. It did not become permanent law, shape Weimar, or abolish the monarchy outright.
questions.hint: Drafted but not enacted.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Where the power lay in the German Empire
questions.learningObjective: Locate power in the German Empire
questions.stem: A design brief asks where decisive power lay in the German Empire of 1871

answer.exemplar: Decisive power rested with the emperor and the chancellor, who controlled foreign and military policy, while the Reichstag had limited budget influence and little control over ministers.

questions.explanation: The emperor and chancellor dominated executive and military affairs. The Reichstag's powers were comparatively narrow.
questions.hint: Emperor and chancellor, not parliament.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: How a German colony was governed

stimulus.body: A colonial ordinance placed a governor appointed from Berlin in charge, with military backing, while local chiefs handled routine matters under supervision.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes an ordinance placing a Berlin-appointed governor over a colony

options.text: Local chiefs held unlimited independent power
The colony ruled itself by direct democracy
Central imperial authority governed through an appointed governor
The colony was governed by a foreign league of nations

questions.explanation: The ordinance shows imperial control via a governor. Self-rule, chiefly independence, and a league of nations do not fit.
questions.hint: Appointed governor under Berlin's authority.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The equality the 1907 civil code brought
questions.stem: A design brief asks what equality the 1907 civil code advanced

options.text: It ended military conscription for all citizens
options.misconception: confuses civil law with military policy

options.text: It granted women full political suffrage
options.misconception: confuses civil code with voting rights

options.text: It abolished all class distinctions in society
options.misconception: overstates legal standardisation as social equality

options.text: It standardised private law across the empire

questions.explanation: The 1907 code unified private law. It did not grant suffrage, abolish class, or end conscription.
questions.hint: Unified private law, not political or social equality.

options.text: An absolute monarchy under an emperor
options.misconception: confuses Weimar with the imperial era

options.text: A federal republic with an elected president
A one-party dictatorship from the start
A confederation with no central government

questions.explanation: Weimar was a federal republic with an elected president. It was not a monarchy, dictatorship, or loose confederation.
questions.hint: Federal republic with president, 1919 onward.

answer.exemplar: After 1945 Germany was divided into occupation zones administered by the Allies, later forming two states, with the Federal Republic in the west and the Democratic Republic in the east.

questions.explanation: Occupation zones came first, then two states. The answer should mention division and the two resulting republics.
questions.hint: Zones first, then two states.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What the November revolution changed

stimulus.body: A 1918 proclamation announced the emperor's abdication, the end of the monarchy, and the transfer of authority to a council of people's deputies.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes a 1918 proclamation on abdication and a council of deputies

options.text: It transferred power solely to the army
options.misconception: confuses military with civilian revolutionary authority

options.text: It restored the emperor with wider powers
It ended the monarchy and created a revolutionary government
It left all institutions completely unchanged
options.misconception: ignores the abdication and new council

questions.explanation: The proclamation ended the monarchy and set up a revolutionary council. Restoration, army rule, and no change contradict it.
questions.hint: Abdication plus new council of deputies.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The structure of the Empire founded in 1871
questions.stem: A design brief asks for the structure of the 1871 German Empire

options.text: A direct democracy of all male citizens
A unitary republic with one national assembly
options.misconception: confuses empire with republic and unitary rule

options.text: A confederation with no emperor at all
A federal monarchy under the Prussian king as emperor

questions.explanation: The 1871 Empire was a federation led by the Prussian king as emperor. It was not a republic, confederation without emperor, or direct democracy.
questions.hint: Federal monarchy, emperor from Prussia.

questions.subject: GERMAN

options.misconception: confuses later loans with the currency reform

options.text: A currency reform introducing the Rentenmark
A return to the gold standard in 1914
options.misconception: uses a wrong date and measure

options.text: The outbreak of a new world war

questions.explanation: The Rentenmark reform stabilised the currency in late 1923. Foreign loans, 1914 gold standard, and war did not end it.
questions.hint: New currency, the Rentenmark.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The conflict between crown and papacy over appointments

stimulus.body: A 1122 agreement lets the emperor invest bishops with secular authority before spiritual consecration by the church, splitting the two aspects of appointment.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes an 1122 agreement splitting secular and spiritual investiture

options.text: It makes the emperor head of the church
options.misconception: confuses secular investiture with ecclesiastical supremacy

options.text: It abolishes the papacy entirely
It is the Concordat of Worms resolving investiture
It ends all royal influence in bishops

questions.explanation: The 1122 compromise is the Concordat of Worms. It neither abolished the papacy, made the emperor church head, nor removed all royal influence.
questions.hint: 1122 compromise on investiture.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The function of an imperial chancery
questions.stem: A design brief asks which document an imperial chancery would issue

options.text: A foreign diplomat's passport
A private merchant's invoice
A peasant's harvest tally
options.misconception: misplaces a local record in the chancery

options.text: A sealed royal charter granting a privilege

questions.explanation: The chancery issued royal documents such as charters. Invoices, tallies, and passports belonged to other spheres.
questions.hint: Royal charters, not commercial or local records.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The legal position of a free city
questions.learningObjective: Contrast free city with subject town
questions.stem: A design brief contrasts a free imperial city with a subject town

options.text: Both answered to the same local bishop
The free city answered to the emperor, the subject town to a prince
The subject town had more autonomy than the free city
Neither owed any allegiance at all

questions.explanation: The distinction is imperial vs princely lordship. Same bishop, reversed autonomy, and no allegiance are wrong.
questions.hint: Emperor vs prince as lord.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The confessional rule of 1555
questions.stem: A design brief asks what the 1555 settlement did not grant

answer.exemplar: It did not grant individuals freedom of conscience; it only let princes choose between Lutheranism and Catholicism for their territories, leaving other confessions unprotected.

questions.explanation: The settlement covered princely choice, not individual conscience or other faiths.
questions.hint: Princely choice only, not individual freedom.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The cause of the peasant revolts of 1524 and 1525

stimulus.body: A rebel pamphlet mixes biblical language with complaints about rents and labour dues, showing both religious framing and economic grievance.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes a rebel pamphlet mixing biblical language with rent complaints

options.text: Only economics mattered; religion was decoration
Only theology mattered; economics were irrelevant
Both religious framing and economic grievance motivated rebels
Neither religion nor economics played any role

questions.explanation: The pamphlet shows both religious language and economic grievance. Reducing to one or denying both misreads it.
questions.hint: Both motives appear in the text.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The cost of a territorial state
questions.stem: A design brief compares the cost of a territorial state with a personal union

options.text: Neither type has any administrative cost
A personal union always costs more in every case
Both cost exactly the same by definition
A territorial state costs more due to permanent institutions

questions.explanation: Territorial states carry permanent institutions and thus higher costs. The other options overgeneralise or deny costs.
questions.hint: Permanent institutions raise cost.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The purpose of the general estate tax
questions.learningObjective: Identify who paid general estate tax
questions.stem: A design brief asks which group a general estate tax fell on

options.text: Only the clergy paid it
options.misconception: narrows a general tax to one estate

options.text: Landholders across estates, not just one group
Only foreigners paid it
No one paid it; it was voluntary

questions.explanation: A general estate tax reached landholders broadly. Clergy-only, foreigners-only, or voluntary readings are wrong.
questions.hint: Broad base across estates.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The printed press and the Enlightenment
questions.stem: A design brief asks what the printed press did not do for the Enlightenment

answer.exemplar: Printing spread ideas but did not by itself create critical thinking; readers, salons, and institutions also had to engage with and debate the printed arguments.

questions.explanation: Printing enabled spread, not automatic critical thought. Engagement and debate were also needed.
questions.hint: Spread, not automatic critique.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The equality established in 1804

stimulus.body: The 1804 code speaks of equality before the law and merit-based careers, while later movements demanded universal suffrage and labour rights.

questions.stem: A design brief contrasts 1804 equality with later rights demands

options.text: 1804 abolished all economic inequality
1804 already included universal suffrage
1804 equality was legal, not political or social
1804 ended all class distinctions immediately

questions.explanation: The code's equality was legal and merit-based. Suffrage, economic equality, and class abolition came later.
questions.hint: Legal and merit-based only.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a grant formula does
questions.stem: A design brief asks where the grant formula appears in a charter

options.text: In the seal's decorative border
Only in the witness list at the end
Only in the dating clause
In the operative clause performing the transfer

questions.explanation: The grant formula sits in the operative clause. Witness lists, dating clauses, and seal decoration are separate parts.
questions.hint: Operative clause, not witness or date.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A grant of market rights
questions.stem: A design brief asks what a market grant did not include

options.text: It allowed unlimited foreign policy
It did not grant full sovereignty over the town
It made the town independent of the emperor
options.misconception: confuses market right with imperial freedom

options.text: It exempted the town from all law

questions.explanation: Market rights were commercial, not sovereign. Foreign policy, imperial independence, and legal exemption exceeded them.
questions.hint: Commerce only, not sovereignty.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A figure in a chronicle
questions.stem: A design brief asks how to cross-check a figure in a chronicle

answer.exemplar: Compare the figure with dated records from other sources, note the chronicler's method and sources, and flag any bias or rounding that could distort the number.

questions.explanation: Cross-checking means comparing with other dated records and noting method and bias.
questions.hint: Compare with other dated records.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The order of two past events

stimulus.body: A text places the founding of a university in 1386 and a printing press in 1455, yet a commentator claims the press caused the university's founding.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes a text placing a university in 1386 and a press in 1455

options.text: The university was founded after the press
The dates are interchangeable
The press could not cause an earlier founding
Both events happened in the same decade

questions.explanation: 1455 cannot cause 1386. The dates are fixed and not interchangeable or simultaneous.
questions.hint: Later event cannot cause earlier one.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a charter is read against
questions.stem: A design brief asks what anachronistic reading to avoid with a charter

options.text: Noting its date and place
Reading it in its original language
Checking its seal for authenticity
Judging its terms by modern legal categories

questions.explanation: Anachronism means applying modern categories. Original language, seal checks, and date noting are sound methods.
questions.hint: Modern categories distort historical meaning.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Why the Peace of Augsburg is called a settlement
questions.stem: A design brief asks which confessions the 1555 settlement recognised

options.text: Calvinism and Anabaptism too
Lutheranism and Catholicism only
All Christian confessions equally
No confessions at all

questions.explanation: Augsburg recognised only Lutheranism and Catholicism. Calvinism, Anabaptism, universal freedom, and no recognition are wrong.
questions.hint: Lutheran and Catholic only.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What an archive takes in
questions.stem: A design brief asks how an archive differs from a museum

answer.exemplar: An archive preserves records created in the course of activity for evidence and research, while a museum collects objects for display and interpretation.

questions.explanation: Archives hold records for evidence and research; museums display objects. The distinction is purpose and material.
questions.hint: Records for evidence vs objects for display.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The steps in the making of a charter

stimulus.body: A manual states that the seal made the charter authentic and that without it the document had no force, even if the text was correct.

questions.stem: A design brief quotes a manual saying the seal made the charter authentic

options.text: The text alone sufficed without a seal
The seal was merely decorative
The seal authenticated the document
The seal replaced the need for witnesses

questions.explanation: The seal authenticated the charter. Decoration, text alone, and replacing witnesses misstate its role.
questions.hint: Seal as authentication, not decoration.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Turning an interest into an archival question
questions.stem: A design brief asks which archival question is best formed

options.text: List every name mentioned anywhere
Tell me everything about the nineteenth century
options.misconception: too broad to guide a search

options.text: Find the oldest document in the archive
What do these 1848 petitions reveal about peasant demands

questions.explanation: A good question targets specific records and evidence. Broad scopes, age-only, and name lists are unfocused.
questions.hint: Specific records and evidence sought.
